newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian government must juggle Russia, NATO.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian government must juggle Russia, NATO.

text.p: Bulgaria's new government to be elected on Saturday will face a delicate balancing act between economic dependence on Russia and its desire for integration with NATO and other Western institutions.
The Bulgarian and Russian prime ministers signed an agreement this week on building and operating gas pipelines for transiting Russian gas through Bulgaria to the Balkans.
Bulgaria still depends on Russian crude, though it has run up big debts now that it no longer comes for free, and Russian companies are interested in several Bulgarian privatisations.
"As far as energy is concerned, the Bulgarians have no choice," said one Sofia-based Western diplomat. "They have to do business with them and they may as well do it on a good commercial basis."

The two countries were close allies in the communist era, but it is paradoxically anti-communist reformers in Bulgaria who now have a more successful relationship with Moscow than do Bulgaria's former communists.
The gas pipelines are vital to Russia's energy expansion plans as well as to the Bulgarian economy but the deal dragged under the less market-oriented former Socialist government.
Ilia Pavlov, president of Bulgaria's powerful Multigroup conglomerate which has a stake in the project, said they had failed to adapt to the new market environment in Russia.
"The Russians have changed their mentality," he said. "We were the first from this region to realise this because we were talking the same business language as them.
"We began by explaining to the government here in Bulgaria that this is not the old Russia, it's a completely new animal, and as you can see we needed three years to finally convince them," he said.
"This is the first time that the administration went to Russia and led the negotiations with the local authorities and as you can see the results were pretty satisfactory."
Investment of $560 million over three to five years will be followed after 2003 by annual transit tax revenue of $100 to $110 million.

The Russians tried to tie the gas deal to a proposal for Bulgaria to buy 14 modern MiG-29SM jet fighters and set up a joint venture in the town of Plovdiv to service MiG planes. Moscow offered Sofia a $450 million credit on easy terms.

"It seems to have been an attempt to keep them tied in to the military industry in Russia. The Russians tried to link it to the gas deal, but (Prime Minister Stefan) Sofianski refused to be bullied," said the Western diplomat.
The deal would have been unlikely to impress the International Monetary Fund, which prescribed a tough programme of reforms to accompany a $657 million credit.

Bulgaria also shows signs of resisting Russian pressure on the sale of a 75 percent stake in the indebted Neftochim refinery. Russia's Rosneft, Neftochim's main supplier, has made its interest clear, but the Privatisation Agency has said the company's many problems would be better solved by a spread of several investors rather than a debt-for-equity deal.
During Sofianski's visit, the two countries also signed a declaration on measures to liberalise trade.

Russia took over some $100 million of the former Soviet Union's debt to Bulgaria after the USSR disintegrated, most of which has already been repaid in supplies for the arms industry, energy and metal works.
Sofianski said Bulgaria hoped to receive some $40 million for the construction of the Sofia underground railway.
"Russia is a great country ruled by great people," Sofianski said on his return from Moscow on Wednesday.
His praise marked a turnround from 1991, when Stoyan Ganev, foreign minister of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), threatened to sue Russia for damage caused by the communist regime.

On the question of NATO expansion, Sofianski said the two sides had to agree to differ. One of the first acts of Sofianski's cabinet was to make a clear statement of their desire to join NATO, an issue on which the Socialists had always been ambivalent for fear of upsetting Moscow.
NATO membership also forms part of the election platform of the UDF, who are expected to form the next government.
"I have not been scolded like that since my schooldays," Sofianski said of Moscow's attitude.
NATO is expected to ignore Russian opposition and invite former East Bloc states to join at its next summit in July.

Bulgaria is highly unlikely to be part of the first wave of expansion, but President Petar Stoyanov wrote to President Bill Clinton this week seeking U.S. backing and warning that by leaving Bulgaria out, the alliance risked creating a "grey area" in the volatile Balkans.
"It's a matter of balancing their interests," said another diplomat. The two are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but the Russians are not easy negotiating partners."
